title: Using Email Well at University
intro: Five short scenarios about using your university email as a professional identity tool. Choose what you would do — you get instant feedback. No account or AI key needed for this part.

scenarios.situation: Ming set up his university email but left the display name as 王明. He emails Dr Smith, who teaches in English and cannot read Chinese.
scenarios.question: What will Dr Smith see, and what should Ming do?

options.text: Switch to "Ming Wang" (or a bilingual name)
options.feedback: Right. Dr Smith sees 王明 in his inbox and may not know who sent it or how to reply politely. At an English-medium university your display name must be readable by everyone — use pinyin or a bilingual name.

options.text: Keep it — the address shows who he is
options.feedback: The address shows the institution, but the display name is what appears in the inbox list and greeting. A name staff can't read makes you harder to reply to and looks careless.

options.text: Email from a personal Gmail instead
options.feedback: No — the university address is the trusted, institution-bound identity. Fix the display name on the university account instead.

probe.question: Quick check: which part of an email appears in the recipient's inbox list and is used to greet you in replies?

options.text: The display name set on the account
options.feedback: Exactly — that's why an unreadable display name is a real problem, whatever the address says.

options.text: Only the email address — the name is never shown
options.feedback: Most mail clients show the display name first and the address only on hover. The name is what people actually see.

options.text: The subject line, which replaces the sender's name
options.feedback: The subject describes the message; the display name identifies the person. Both matter, but they do different jobs.

bullets: Ming's display name is still 王明
The display name is what the inbox shows

scenarios.situation: Anna wants to know when the essay is due. She opens a new email to her teacher.
scenarios.question: What should Anna do first?

options.text: Check the syllabus and announcements first
options.feedback: Exactly. If the answer is already in the materials, emailing the teacher signals you haven't done the work — and wastes their time.

options.text: Send a short, polite email now
options.feedback: Politeness doesn't fix the real problem: asking something already answered in the syllabus is disrespectful of the teacher's time and exposes that you didn't check.

options.text: Ask a classmate to email for her
options.feedback: Same problem, delegated. Check the course materials first — the due date is almost certainly there.

probe.question: Quick check: why does emailing a question that the syllabus already answers create a bad impression?

options.text: It shows the student didn't check the materials and shifts that work onto the teacher
options.feedback: Right — it costs the teacher time and tells them you skipped the first step every student is expected to take.

options.text: University rules forbid teachers from repeating information by email
options.feedback: There's no such rule — teachers can repeat information; the issue is what the question reveals about your effort.

options.text: Questions to teachers are only allowed during scheduled office hours
options.feedback: Email questions are fine at any reasonable time — as long as the answer isn't already in the materials.

bullets: Anna wants the essay due date
She is about to email the teacher

scenarios.situation: Ben is writing a formal email to Professor Sarah Lee, whom he has never met.
scenarios.question: Which greeting is appropriate?

options.text: Dear Professor Lee,
options.feedback: Correct — formal greeting is Title + SURNAME.

options.text: Dear Professor Sarah,
options.feedback: Title + first name is always wrong ("Dr John", "Professor Sarah"). Use Title + surname: Professor Lee.

options.text: Hi Sarah!
options.feedback: First name alone is only acceptable when the teacher is clearly informal or has invited it — never in a first formal email.

probe.question: Quick check: in formal English greetings, a title (Dr, Professor) combines with…

options.text: The surname only — "Professor Lee"
options.feedback: Yes. Title + surname is the safe formal pattern in English.

options.text: The first name only — "Professor Sarah"
options.feedback: Title + first name is a very common mistake — it is always wrong in formal English.

options.text: Either one — both are equally formal
options.feedback: They are not interchangeable: only title + surname is formal. Title + first name is always wrong.

bullets: First email to Professor Sarah Lee

scenarios.situation: Carla's university address is s2409831@uni.edu. She notices staff emails look like jane.chan@uni.edu.
scenarios.question: What should Carla do?

options.text: Request a readable alias like carla.gomez@
options.feedback: Yes — most universities allow this. A student-number address is functional but anonymous; a readable alias makes every email you send more professional.

options.text: Accept it — student addresses are fixed
options.feedback: Most universities allow a readable alias alongside the student-number address. It's worth the five minutes to set up.

options.text: Add her name to every subject line
options.feedback: That clutters subject lines. Fix the root cause: set a readable alias and a proper display name.

probe.question: Quick check: what is an email alias?

options.text: An additional address that delivers to the same mailbox
options.feedback: Right — same inbox, better first impression on everything you send.

options.text: A second mailbox that needs its own separate password
options.feedback: No new mailbox or password — an alias is just another name for the mailbox you already have.

options.text: A nickname that only appears inside the university portal
options.feedback: An alias is a real, usable email address — anyone inside or outside the university can send to it.

bullets: Every email carries this first impression

scenarios.situation: Dev's inbox shows 1,247 unread emails. He says: "I read the important ones — the rest can sit there."
scenarios.question: What does this actually reveal?

options.text: He has no email system — triage is missing
options.feedback: Right. A four-digit unread count means important mail WILL eventually be missed. Triage is a study skill, not a tidiness preference.

options.text: Nothing — unread counts are cosmetic
options.feedback: An unmanaged inbox means no reliable way to catch deadlines, room changes, or feedback. It's a time-management failure waiting to surface.

options.text: He should delete everything each term
options.feedback: Bankruptcy without a new habit repeats the cycle. The fix is the daily triage habit: read → act → archive.

probe.question: Quick check: what is the goal of a daily email triage habit?

options.text: Every message gets read, acted on, or archived — unread stays near zero
options.feedback: Exactly — the point is that nothing important can hide, because nothing sits unprocessed.

options.text: Replying to every email within five minutes of it arriving
options.feedback: Triage is about processing, not instant replies — many messages just need to be read and archived.

options.text: Keeping messages unread on purpose so urgent ones stand out
options.feedback: That's the failure mode, not the system — with 1,000+ unread, nothing stands out anymore.

finalCheck.question: Your display name at an English-medium university should be…

options.text: English (pinyin) or bilingual
Chinese characters only
A casual nickname

finalCheck.question: Before emailing a teacher a question, you should…

options.text: Check syllabus, notes and announcements
Email immediately — it's faster
Ask in several channels at once

finalCheck.question: Which greeting pattern is ALWAYS wrong?

options.text: Dr John (title + first name)
Dear Dr Chan (title + surname)
Dear Professor Lee (title + surname)

finalCheck.question: A readable address alias (name@ instead of s123456@)…

options.text: Is usually available and worth setting up
Requires a separate second mailbox
Is reserved for staff accounts only
No email system — a time-management problem
Harmless newsletter build-up
The spam filter needs adjusting

agent.name: Email Essentials Coach
agent.job: Turn your rough points into one polished, professional university email.
agent.knowledge: The etiquette rules from Part A — readable names, Title + surname greetings, homework-first questions, professional tone.
agent.tools: A language model guided by this pack's SKILL and knowledge files.
workflow: Check it against the etiquette rules
Deliver the email with key choices explained
agent.guardrails: Sticks to university email tasks only; never invents facts or writes fake excuses on your behalf.
agent.evaluation: You rate each deliverable 1–5 and may request one revision — that feedback loop is how the agent improves.

intake.label: Key points to include
